[[Image:peridynamics-neck.jpg|thumb|Computer model of the necking of an aluminum rod under tension. Colors indicate temperature increase due to plastic heating. Calculation performed with the Emu computer code using peridynamic state-based framework.]]'''Peridynamics''' is a [[Nonlocal operator|non-local]] formulation of [[continuum mechanics]] that is oriented toward [[deformation (engineering)|deformation]]s with discontinuities, especially [[fracture]]s.  Originally, ''bond-based'' peridynamic was introduced,<ref name="silling">{{Cite journal |last=Silling |first=S.A. |date= January 2000 |title=Reformulation of elasticity theory for discontinuities and long-range forces |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022509699000290 |journal=Journal of the Mechanics and Physics of Solids |language=en |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=175–209 |doi=10.1016/S0022-5096(99)00029-0|bibcode=2000JMPSo..48..175S |s2cid=122055539 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> wherein, internal interaction forces between a material point and all the other ones with which it can interact, are modeled as a central [[Force field (chemistry)|force field]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dimola |first1=Nunzio |last2=Coclite |first2=Alessandro |last3=Fanizza |first3=Giuseppe |last4=Politi |first4=Tiziano |date=2022-10-23 |title=Bond-based peridynamics, a survey prospecting nonlocal theories of fluid-dynamics |journal=Advances in Continuous and Discrete Models |language=en |volume=2022 |issue=1 |article-number=60 |doi=10.1186/s13662-022-03732-6 |issn=2731-4235|arxiv=2207.06194 |doi-access=free }}</ref> This type of force field can be imagined as a mesh of bonds connecting each point of the body with every other interacting point within a certain distance which depends on a material property, called the ''peridynamic horizon''. Later, to overcome bond-based framework limitations for the material [[Poisson's ratio]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last1=Madenci |first1=Erdogan |title=Peridynamic theory and its applications|author2-link=Erkan Oterkus |last2=Oterkus |first2=Erkan |date=2014 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-4614-8464-6 |location=New York, NY |pages=19–43}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Macek |first1=Richard W. |last2=Silling |first2=Stewart A. |date=November 2007 |title=Peridynamics via finite element analysis |journal=Finite Elements in Analysis and Design |volume=43 |issue=15 |pages=1169–1178 |doi=10.1016/j.finel.2007.08.012 |osti=1725746 |issn=0168-874X}}</ref> (<math>1/3</math> for [[plane stress]] and <math>1/4</math> for [[Infinitesimal strain theory|plane strain]] in two-dimensional configurations; <math>1/4</math> for three-dimensional ones), ''state-base'' peridynamics, has been formulated.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Silling |first1=S. A. |last2=Epton |first2=M. |last3=Weckner |first3=O. |last4=Xu |first4=J. |last5=Askari |first5=E. |date=2007-08-08 |title=Peridynamic States and Constitutive Modeling |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10659-007-9125-1 |journal=Journal of Elasticity |language=en |volume=88 |issue=2 |pages=151–184 |doi=10.1007/s10659-007-9125-1 |s2cid=30571789 |issn=0374-3535|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Its characteristic feature is that the force exchanged between a point and another one is influenced by the deformation state of all other bonds relative to its interaction zone.<ref name="silling" />

The characteristic feature of peridynamics, which makes it different from classical local mechanics, is the presence of finite-range bonds between any two points of the material body: it is a feature that approaches such formulations as discrete meso-scale theories of matter.<ref name="silling" />

== Etymology ==
The term ''peridynamic'', as an adjective, was proposed in the year 2000 and comes from the prefix ''peri-'', which means ''all around'', ''near'', or ''surrounding''; and the root ''dyna'', which means ''force'' or ''power''. The term ''peridynamics'', as a noun, is a shortened form of the phrase ''peridynamic model of solid mechanics.''<ref name="silling" />

==Purpose==

A fracture is a [[mathematical singularity]] to which the classical equations of [[continuum mechanics]] cannot be applied directly. The peridynamic theory has been proposed with the purpose of mathematically models fractures formation and dynamic in elastic materials.<ref name="silling" /> It is founded on [[integral equation]]s, in contrast with classical continuum mechanics, which is based on [[partial differential equation]]s. Since [[partial derivative]]s do not exist on crack surfaces<ref name=silling /> and other geometric [[Mathematical singularity|singularities]], the classical equations of [[continuum mechanics]] cannot be applied directly when such features are present in a [[deformation (engineering)|deformation]]. The integral equations of the peridynamic theory hold true also on singularities and can be applied directly, because they do not require partial derivatives. The ability to apply the same equations directly at all points in a [[mathematical model]] of a deforming structure helps the peridynamic approach to avoid the need for the special techniques of [[fracture mechanics]] like [[Extended finite element method|xFEM]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Javili |first1=Ali |last2=Morasata |first2=Rico |last3=Oterkus |first3=Erkan |last4=Oterkus |first4=Selda |date=November 2019 |title=Peridynamics review |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1081286518803411 |journal=Mathematics and Mechanics of Solids |language=en |volume=24 |issue=11 |pages=3714–3739 |doi=10.1177/1081286518803411 |s2cid=162176799 |issn=1081-2865|hdl=11693/53217 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> For example, in peridynamics, there is no need for a separate crack growth law based on a [[stress intensity factor]].<ref name=":28" />

== Definition and basic terminology ==
[[File:Kinematics of peridynamic theory.png|thumb|(a) Kinematics of material body <math>\Omega_t</math> within peridynamic theory. (b) Representation of peridynamic horizon of <math>\bf x</math>.|377x377px]]
In the context of peridynamic theory, physical bodies are treated as constituted by a continuous points mesh which can exchange long-range mutual interaction forces, within a maximum and well established distance <math>\delta > 0</math>: the ''peridynamic horizon'' radius.  This perspective approaches much more to [[molecular dynamics]] than [[Macroscopic scale|macroscopic]] bodies, and as a consequence, is not based on the concept of [[Cauchy stress tensor|stress tensor]] (which is a local concept) and drift toward the notion of ''pairwise force'' that a material point <math>{\bf x}</math> exchanges within its peridynamic horizon. With a [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]] point of view, suited for small displacements, the peridynamic horizon is considered fixed in the reference configuration and, then, deforms with the body.<ref name=":1" /> Consider a material body represented by <math>\Omega \subset \R^{n}</math>, where <math>n</math> can be either 1, 2 or 3. The body has a positive [[density]] <math>\rho</math>. Its reference configuration at the initial time is denoted by <math>\Omega_{0} \subset \R^{n}</math>. The reference configuration can either be the [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]]-free configuration or a specific configuration of the body chosen as a reference. In the context of peridynamics, every point in <math>\Omega</math> interacts with all the points <math>{\bf x}'</math> within a certain neighborhood defined by <math>d({\bf x},{\bf x}')\leq\delta</math>, where <math>\delta > 0</math> and <math>d(\cdot,\cdot)</math> represents a suitable [[Distance (mathematics)|distance]] function on <math>\Omega_0</math>. This neighborhood is often referred to as <math>B_\delta({\bf x})</math> in the literature. It is commonly known as the ''horizon''<ref name=":28"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ren |first1=Huilong |last2=Zhuang |first2=Xiaoying |author2-link= Xioaying Zhuang |last3=Cai |first3=Yongchang |last4=Rabczuk |first4=Timon |date=2016-12-21 |title=Dual-horizon peridynamics: Dual-horizon peridynamics |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/nme.5257 |journal=International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering |language=en |volume=108 |issue=12 |pages=1451–1476 |doi=10.1002/nme.5257|arxiv=1506.05146 |s2cid=117201049 }}</ref> or the ''family'' of <math>{\bf x}</math>.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Ziguang |last2=Bakenhus |first2=Drew |last3=Bobaru |first3=Florin |date=November 2016 |title=A constructive peridynamic kernel for elasticity |journal=Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering |language=en |volume=311 |pages=356–373 |doi=10.1016/j.cma.2016.08.012|bibcode=2016CMAME.311..356C |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The [[kinematics]] of <math>{\bf x}</math> is described in terms of its displacement from the reference position, denoted as <math>{\bf u}({\bf x}, t): \Omega_{0} \times \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n}</math>. Consequently, the position of <math>{\bf x}</math> at a specific time <math>t</math> is determined by <math>{\bf y}({\bf x},t):= {\bf x}+{\bf u}({\bf x}, t)</math>. Furthermore, for each pair of interacting points, the change in the length of the bond relative to the initial configuration is tracked over time through the relative [[Deformation (physics)|strain]] <math>s({\bf x},{\bf x}',t)</math>, which can be expressed as:

<math> s\left({\bf x}, {\bf x}', t\right)=\frac{\left|{\bf u}\left({\bf x}^{\prime}, t\right)-{\bf u}({\bf x}, t)\right|}{\left|{\bf x}^{\prime}-{\bf x}\right|}, </math>

where <math> |\cdot| </math> denotes the [[Euclidean space|Euclidean norm]]<ref name=":1" /> and <math> {\bf x}' \in B_{\delta}({\bf x}) \cap \Omega_0 </math>.

The interaction between any <math>\bf x</math> and <math>\bf x'</math> is referred to as a ''bond''. These pairwise bonds have varying lengths over time in response to the force per unit volume squared, denoted as<ref name=":1" />

<math>{\bf f}\equiv {\bf f}({\bf x}',{\bf x},{\bf u}({\bf x}'),{\bf u}({\bf x}),t)</math>.

This force is commonly known as the ''pairwise force function'' or ''peridynamic [[Integral kernel|kernel]]'', and it encompasses all the [[Constitutive equation|constitutive]] (material-dependent) properties. It describes how the internal forces depend on the deformation. It's worth noting that the dependence of <math>{\bf u}</math> on <math>t</math> has been omitted here for the sake of simplicity in notation. Additionally, an external forcing term, <math>\mathbf{b}({\bf x},t)</math>, is introduced, which results in the following equation of motion, representing the fundamental equation of peridynamics:<ref name=":1" />

<math> {\rho {\bf u}_{tt}({\bf x},t) = {\bf F}({\bf x},t)}\, . </math>

where the integral term <math>{\bf F}({\bf x},t)</math> is the sum of all of the internal and external per-unit-volume forces acting on <math>{\bf x}</math>:

<math> {{\bf F}({\bf x}, t):=\int_{\Omega_0 \cap B_{\delta}({\bf x})} {\bf f}\left( {\bf x}', {\bf x}, {\bf u} \left( {\bf x}' \right),{\bf u}({\bf x}) \right) dV_{{\bf x}'}+{\bf b}({\bf x}, t)}\, . </math>

The [[Vector (geometric)|vector]] valued [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>\bf f</math> is the [[force density]] that <math>\bf x'</math> exerts on <math>\bf x</math>. This force density depends on the relative displacement and relative position vectors between <math>\bf x'</math> and <math>\bf x</math>. The [[dimension]] of <math>\bf f</math> is <math>[N/m^6]</math>.<ref name=":1" />

== Bond-based peridynamics ==
In this formulation of peridynamics, the kernel is determined by the nature of internal forces and physical constraints that governs the interaction between only two material points. For the sake of brevity, the following quantities are defined  <math>{\bf {\bf \xi}} := {\bf x}'-{\bf x}</math> and <math>{\bf \eta}:={\bf u}({\bf x}')-{\bf u}({\bf x})</math> so that<ref name="silling" />

<math>{\bf f}({\bf x}'-{\bf x},{\bf u}({\bf x}')-{\bf u}({\bf x})) \equiv \bf{f}({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})</math>

=== Action and reaction principle ===
For any  <math>\bf x</math>   and  <math>\bf x'</math>   belonging to the neighborhood  <math>B_\delta({\bf x})</math>, the following relationship holds:  <math>{\bf f}(-\eta, -\xi) = -{\bf f}(\eta, \xi)</math>  . This expression reflects the principle of action and reaction, commonly known as [[Newton's laws of motion|Newton's third law.]] It guarantees the conservation of [[Momentum|linear momentum]] in a system composed of mutually interacting particles.<ref name="silling" />

=== Angular momentum conservation ===

For any <math>\bf{x}</math>  and <math>\bf{x}'</math>  belonging to the neighborhood <math>B_\delta({\bf x})</math>, the following condition holds: <math>(\xi + \eta) \times {\bf f}(\xi, \eta) = 0</math> . This condition arises from considering the relative deformed ray-[[Euclidean vector|vector]] connecting <math>\bf{x}</math>  and <math>\bf{x}'</math> as <math>\xi + \eta</math> . The condition is satisfied [[if and only if]] the pairwise force density vector has the same direction as the relative deformed ray-vector. In other words, <math>{\bf f}(\xi, \eta) = f(\xi, \eta)(\xi + \eta)</math>  for all <math>\xi</math>  and <math>\eta</math> , where <math>f(\xi, \eta)</math>  is a scalar-valued function.<ref name="silling" />

=== Hyperelastic material ===
An [[Hyperelastic material|hyperelastic]] material is a material with constitutive relation such that:<ref name="silling" />

<math>

\int_{\Gamma} {\bf f}({\bf \xi}, {\bf \eta}) \cdot d {\bf \eta}=0\, , \quad \forall \text{ closed curve } \Gamma, \ \ \ \ \forall{\bf \xi}\neq \bf{0},

</math>

or, equivalently, by [[Stokes' theorem]]

<math>

\nabla_{{\bf \eta}} \times {\bf f}({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})=\bf{0}\,
</math>  ,<math>\forall \, {\bf \xi}, \, {\bf \eta}</math>

and, thus,

<math>

{\bf f}({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})=\nabla_{{\bf \eta}} \Phi({\bf \xi}, \, {\bf \eta}) \, \forall {\bf \xi}, \,  {\bf \eta} \, .

</math>

In the equation above <math> \Phi({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta}) </math> is the scalar valued [[Scalar potential|potential function]] in <math> C^2(\R^n \setminus\bf{\{0\}} \times \R^n) </math>.<ref name="silling" /> Due to the necessity of satisfying [[angular momentum]] conservation, the condition below on the scalar valued function <math> f({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta}) </math> follows<ref name="silling" />

<math>

\frac{\partial f({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})}{\partial {\bf \eta}}=g({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})({\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta}).

</math>

where <math> g({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta}) </math> is a scalar valued function. Integrating both sides of the equation, the following condition on <math> g({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta}) </math> is obtained<ref name="silling" />

<math>{\bf f}({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})= h(| {\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta}|,{\bf \xi})({\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta})</math>,   

for <math>h(| {\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta}|,{\bf \xi})</math> a scalar valued function. The [[Elasticity (physics)|elastic]] nature of <math> {\bf f} </math> is evident: the interaction force depends only on the initial relative position between points <math> {\bf x} </math> and <math> {\bf x}' </math> and the modulus of their relative position, <math> | {\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta}| </math>, in the deformed configuration <math> \Omega_t</math> at time <math>t</math>. Applying the [[isotropy]] hypothesis, the dependence on vector <math> {\bf \xi} </math> can be substituted with a dependence on its modulus <math> |{\bf \xi}| </math>,<ref name="silling" />

<math>{\bf f}({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})=h(| {\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta}|,|{\bf \xi}|)({\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta}). </math>

Bond forces can, thus, be considered as modeling a spring net that connects each point  <math> {\bf x} \in \Omega_0 </math> pairwise with <math> {\bf x}' \in B_{\delta}({\bf x}) \cap \Omega_0 </math>.

=== Linear elastic material ===
If <math> |{\bf \eta}| \ll 1 </math>, the peridynamic kernel can be linearised around <math> {\bf \eta}=\bf{0} </math>:<ref name="silling" />

<math>{\bf f}({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})\approx {\bf f}({\bf \xi},\bf{0})+\left. \frac{\partial {\bf f}({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})}{\partial{\bf \eta}}\right|_{{\bf \eta}=\bf{0}}{\bf \eta};</math>

then, a second-order ''micro-modulus'' [[tensor]] can be defined as

<math>{\bf C}({\bf \xi})=\left. \frac{\partial {\bf f}({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})}{\partial {\bf \eta}}\right|_{{\bf \eta}=\bf{0}}={\bf \xi} \otimes \left.\frac{\partial f({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta})}{\partial {\bf \eta}}\right|_{{\bf \eta}=\bf{0}}+f_0I</math>

where <math> f_0:=f({\bf \xi},{\bf 0}) </math> and <math>I</math> is the identity tensor. Following application of linear momentum balance, elasticity and isotropy condition, the micro-modulus tensor can be expressed in this form<ref name="silling" />

<math>{\bf C}({\bf \xi})=\lambda(|{\bf \xi}|){\bf \xi} \otimes {\bf \xi}+f_0I.</math>

Therefore, for a linearised hyperelastic material, its peridynamic kernel holds the following structure<ref name="silling" />

<math>{\bf f}({\bf \xi},{\bf \eta}) \approx {\bf f}({\bf \xi},{\bf 0})+\left(\lambda(|{\bf \xi}|){\bf \xi} \otimes {\bf \xi}+f_0I\right){\bf \eta}.</math>

=== Expressions for the peridynamic kernel ===

The peridynamic kernel is a versatile function that characterizes the constitutive behavior of materials within the framework of peridynamic theory. One commonly employed formulation of the kernel is used to describe a class of materials known as ''prototype micro-elastic brittle'' (PMB) materials. In the case of isotropic PMB materials, the pairwise force is assumed to be linearly proportional to the finite stretch<ref name=":28" /> experienced by the material, defined as

<math> s:= (|{\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta}|-|{\bf \xi}|)/|{\bf \xi}| </math>,

so that

<math>
\mathbf{f}({\bf \eta}, {\bf \xi})=f(|{\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta}|,|{\bf \xi}|) \bf{n},
</math>

where

<math> \bf{n}:=({\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta})/|{\bf \xi} + {\bf \eta}| </math>

and where the scalar function <math> f </math> is defined as follow<ref name=":28">{{Cite journal |last1=Silling |first1=S.A. |last2=Askari |first2=E. |date=June 2005 |title=A meshfree method based on the peridynamic model of solid mechanics |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0045794905000805 |journal=Computers & Structures |language=en |volume=83 |issue=17–18 |pages=1526–1535 |doi=10.1016/j.compstruc.2004.11.026|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math>
f=cs\mu(s,t)=c \; \frac{|{\bf \xi}+{\bf \eta}|-|{\bf \xi}|}{|{\bf \xi}|}\mu(s,t),
</math> with

<math>
\mu(s,t)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
1\, , & \text { if } s\left(t^{\prime}, {\bf \xi}\right)<s_{0}\, , \\
0\, , & \text { otherwise, }
\end{array}\ \ \ \  \text { for all } 0 \leq t^{\prime} \leq t\right.;
</math>

The constant <math> c </math> is referred to as the ''micro-modulus constant'', and the function <math> \mu(s, t) </math> serves to indicate whether, at a given time <math> t'\leq t </math>, the bond stretch <math> s </math> associated with the pair <math> ({\bf x,\,x'}) </math> has surpassed the critical value <math> s_0 </math>. If the critical value is exceeded, the bond is considered ''broken'', and a pairwise force of zero is assigned for all <math> t \geq t' </math>.<ref name="silling" />

After a comparison between the [[Strain energy density function|strain energy density]] value obtained under isotropic extension respectively employing peridynamics and classical continuum theory framework, the physical coherent value of micro-modulus <math> c </math> can be found<ref name=":28"/>

<math>
c=\frac{18 k}{\pi \delta^{4}},
</math>

where <math>k</math> is the material [[bulk modulus]].

Following the same approach<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bobaru |first1=Florin |last2=Duangpanya |first2=Monchai |date=September 2010 |title=The peridynamic formulation for transient heat conduction |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0017931010002668 |journal=International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer |language=en |volume=53 |issue=19–20 |pages=4047–4059 |doi=10.1016/j.ijheatmasstransfer.2010.05.024|bibcode=2010IJHMT..53.4047B |url-access=subscription }}</ref> the micro-modulus constant <math> c </math> can be extended to <math> c({\bf \xi},\delta) </math>, where <math> c </math> is now a ''micro-modulus function''. This function provides a more detailed description of how the intensity of pairwise forces is distributed over the peridynamic horizon <math> B_{\delta}({\bf x}) </math>. Intuitively, the intensity of forces decreases as the distance between <math>\bf x</math> and <math>{\bf x}' \in B_{\delta}({\bf x}) </math> increases, but the specific manner in which this decrease occurs can vary.

The micro-modulus function is expressed as<ref name=":26" />

<math>
    c({\bf \xi},\delta):=c(\bf{0},\delta)k({\bf \xi},\delta)\, ,
</math>

where the constant <math> c(\bf{0},\delta) </math> is obtained by comparing peridynamic strain density with the classical mechanical theories;<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Zhiyong |last2=Woody Ju |first2=J. |last3=Su |first3=Guoshao |last4=Huang |first4=Xiaohua |last5=Li |first5=Shuang |last6=Zhai |first6=Lianjun |date=July 2019 |title=Influence of micro-modulus functions on peridynamics simulation of crack propagation and branching in brittle materials |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0013794419303406 |journal=Engineering Fracture Mechanics |language=en |volume=216 |article-number=106498 |doi=10.1016/j.engfracmech.2019.106498|s2cid=197621064 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> <math> k({\bf \xi},\delta) </math> is a function defined on <math> \Omega_0 </math> with the following properties (given the restrictions of momentum conservation and isotropy)<ref name=":26">{{Cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Dan |last2=Lu |first2=Guangda |last3=Wang |first3=Chongwen |last4=Qiao |first4=Pizhong |date=June 2015 |title=An extended peridynamic approach for deformation and fracture analysis |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0013794415002039 |journal=Engineering Fracture Mechanics |language=en |volume=141 |pages=196–211 |doi=10.1016/j.engfracmech.2015.04.036|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math>
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
k({\bf \xi}, \delta)=k(-{\bf \xi}, \delta)\, , \\
\lim _{{\bf \xi} \rightarrow \bf{0}} k({\bf \xi}, \delta)=\max_{{\bf \xi}\ \in \R^n}\{ k({\bf \xi},\delta)\}\, , \\
\lim _{{\bf \xi} \rightarrow \delta} k({\bf \xi}, \delta)=0 \, ,\\
\int_{\R^n} \lim _{\delta \rightarrow 0} k({\bf \xi}, \delta) d {\bf x}=\int_{\R^n} \Delta({\bf \xi}) d {\bf x}=1\, ,
\end{array}\right.
</math>

where <math> \Delta({\bf \xi}) </math> is the [[Dirac delta function]]. [[File:Widely_employed_Peridynamics_Micromodulus.png|alt=Widely employed Peridynamics Micromodulus|thumb|353x353px|Pictorial representation of some widely used micro-modulus function <math>
    c({\bf \xi},\delta)=c(\bf{0},\delta)k({\bf \xi},\delta)
</math>.]]

==== Cylindrical micro-modulus ====
The simplest expression for the micro-modulus function is<ref name=":26" />

<math>c(\bf{0},\delta)k({\bf \xi},\delta)=c\bf{1}_{B_{\delta}({\bf x}')} </math>,

where <math> \bf{1}_{A} </math>: <math> X \rightarrow \R </math> is the [[indicator function]] of the subset <math> A \subset X </math>, defined as

<math>
\mathbf{1}_{A}(x):= \begin{cases} 1, & x \in A\, , \\ 0, & x \notin A\, , \end{cases}\; \;;
</math>

==== Triangular micro-modulus ====
It is characterized by <math> k({\bf \xi},\delta) </math> to a be a [[Linear function (calculus)|linear function]]<ref name=":27">{{Cite journal |last1=Ha |first1=Youn Doh |last2=Bobaru |first2=Florin |date=March 2010 |title=Studies of dynamic crack propagation and crack branching with peridynamics |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10704-010-9442-4 |journal=International Journal of Fracture |language=en |volume=162 |issue=1–2 |pages=229–244 |doi=10.1007/s10704-010-9442-4 |s2cid=8462707 |issn=0376-9429|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math>
    k({\bf \xi},\delta)= \left( 1-\frac{|{\bf \xi}|}{\delta} \right)\bf{1}_{B_{\delta}({\bf x}')}. 
</math>

==== Normal micro-modulus ====
If one wants to reflects the fact that most common discrete physical systems are characterized by a [[Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution|Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution]], in order to include this behavior in peridynamics, the following expression for <math> k({\bf \xi},\delta) </math> can be utilized<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kilic |first=Bahattin |date=2008 |title=Peridynamic Theory for Progressive Failure Prediction in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Materials |url=https://repository.arizona.edu/handle/10150/193658 |language=EN}}</ref>

<math>
k({\bf \xi},\delta)=e^{-(|{\bf \xi}| / \delta)^{2}}\bf{1}_{B_{\delta}({\bf x}')};
</math>

==== Quartic micro-modulus ====
In the literature one can find also the following expression for the <math> k({\bf \xi},\delta) </math>function<ref name=":26" />

<math>
k({\bf \xi}, \delta)=\left(1-\left(\frac{\xi}{\delta}\right)^{2}\right)^{2}\bf{1}_{B_{\delta}({\bf x}')}.
</math>

Overall, depending on the specific material property to be modeled, there exists a wide range of expressions for the micro-modulus and, in general, for the peridynamic kernel. The above list is, thus, not exhaustive.<ref name=":26" />

==Damage==
[[File:Inner-force.png|thumb|Representation of peridynamic pairwise force function <math>{\bf f}(\xi, \eta)</math> with bond-breaking function <math>\mu(s,t) </math>; after the critical stretch value <math>s_0 </math> is exceeded, the bond is considered broken and no force exists between the two involved material points.|350x350px]][[Damage mechanics|Damage]] is incorporated in the pairwise force function by allowing bonds to break when their elongation exceeds some prescribed value. After a bond breaks, it no longer sustains any force, and the endpoints are effectively disconnected from each other. When a bond breaks, the force it was carrying is redistributed to other bonds that have not yet broken. This increased load makes it more likely that these other bonds will break. The process of bond breakage and load redistribution, leading to further breakage, is how cracks grow in the peridynamic model.<ref name=":28" />

Analytically, the bond breaking is specified inside the expression of the peridynamic kernel, by the function<ref name=":28" />

<math>
\mu(s,t)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
1\, , & \text { if } s\left(t^{\prime}, {\bf \xi}\right)<s_{0}\, , \\
0\, , & \text { otherwise, }
\end{array}\ \ \ \  \text { for all } 0 \leq t^{\prime} \leq t\right.;
</math>

If the graph of <math>{\bf f}(s,t)</math> versus bond stretching <math>s</math> is plotted, the action of the bond breaking function <math>\mu</math> in the fracture formation is clear. However, not only abrupt fracture can be modeled in the peridynamic framework and more general expressions for <math>\mu</math> can be employed.<ref name=":28"/>

== State-based peridynamics ==
The theory described above assumes that each peridynamic bond responds independently of all the others. This is an oversimplification for most materials and leads to restrictions on the types of materials that can be modeled. In particular, this assumption implies that any [[Linear elastic material|isotropic linear elastic solid]] is restricted to a [[Poisson ratio]] of 1/4.<ref name=":1" />

To address this lack of generality, the idea of ''peridynamic states'' was introduced. This framework allows the force density in each bond to depend on the stretches in all the bonds connected to its endpoints, in addition to its own stretch. For example, the force in a bond could depend on the net volume changes at the endpoints. The effect of this volume change, relative to the effect of the bond stretch, determines the [[Poisson's ratio|Poisson ratio]]. With peridynamic states, any material that can be modeled within the standard theory of [[continuum mechanics]] can be modeled as a peridynamic material, while retaining the advantages of the peridynamic theory for fracture.<ref name=":2" />

Mathematically the equation of the internal and external force term

<math> {{\bf F}({\bf x}, t):=\int_{\Omega_0 \cap B_{\delta}({\bf x})} {\bf f}\left( {\bf x}', {\bf x}, {\bf u} \left( {\bf x}' \right),{\bf u}({\bf x}) \right) dV_{{\bf x}'}+{\bf b}({\bf x}, t)}\, . </math>

used in the bond-based formulations is substituted by<ref name=":2" /><math>{\bf F}({\bf x}, t) := \int_{B_\delta({\bf x})}\left\{\underline{\mathbf{T}}[\mathbf{x}, t]\left\langle\mathbf{x}^{\prime}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle-\underline{\mathbf{T}}\left[\mathbf{x}^{\prime}, t\right]\left\langle\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right\rangle\right\} d V_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}+\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x}, t), </math>

where <math> \underline{\mathbf{T}} </math> is the force vector state field.

A general m-order state <math>  \underline{\mathbf{A}}\langle\cdot\rangle: B_\delta({\bf x}) \rightarrow \mathcal{L}_m . </math> is a [[mathematical object]] similar to a [[tensor]], with the exception that it is<ref name=":2" />
*in general non-linear;
*in general non-continuous;
*is not finite dimensional.
Vector states are states of order equal to 2. For so called ''simple material'', <math>\underline{\mathbf{T}}</math> is defined as

<math>\underline{\mathbf{T}}:=\underline{\mathbf{\hat{T}}}(\underline{\mathbf{Y}})</math>

where <math>\underline{\mathbf{\hat{T}}}: \mathcal{V} \rightarrow \mathcal{V} </math> is a [[Riemann integral|Riemann-integrable]] function on <math>B_\delta({\bf x})</math> , and  <math>\underline{\mathbf{Y}}</math> is called  ''deformation vector state field'' and is defined by the following relation<ref name=":2" />

<math>

\underline{\mathbf{Y}}[\mathbf{x}, t]\langle\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle=\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}+\boldsymbol{\xi}, t)-\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}, t) \quad \forall \mathbf{x} \in \Omega_0, \xi \in B_{\delta}({\bf x}), t \geq 0

</math>

thus <math> \underline{\mathbf{Y}}\left\langle\mathbf{x}^{\prime}-\mathbf{x}\right\rangle </math> is the image of the bond <math> \mathbf{x}^{\prime}-\mathbf{x} </math> under the deformation

such that

<math>
\underline{\mathbf{Y}}\langle\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle=\mathbf{0} \text { if and only if } \boldsymbol{\xi}=\mathbf{0},

</math>

which means that two distinct particles never occupy the same point as the deformation progresses.<ref name=":2" />

It can be proved<ref name=":2" /> that balance of linear momentum follow from the definition of <math>{\bf F}({\bf x, \, t })</math>, while, if the constitutive relation is such that

<math>\int_{B_\delta({\bf x})} \underline{\mathbf{Y}}\langle\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle \times \underline{\mathbf{T}}\langle\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle d V_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}=0 \quad \forall \underline{\mathbf{Y}} \in \mathcal{V}</math>

the force vector state field satisfy balance of angular momentum.<ref name=":2" />
